Source:
Decision aid
What is it: text, image, audio, video or a chatbot?
Images, audio, video: are BOTH deepfake criteria met – reference to real or plausible persons, places or events AND potential to deceive?
Texts: is it about a matter of public interest, and is there no substantive human review?
Product images: does the AI change the product itself or its use?
If yes: label visibly. In case of doubt, label voluntarily.
Obligations by content type

Texts: label if published without review and intended to inform the public on matters of public interest (public safety, health, environment, consumer protection, crisis communication, political and economic questions). Purely promotional texts usually not, unless they look like independent reporting.
Images: there is no general obligation for AI images – deepfakes must be labelled. Realistic fictitious landscapes are disputed; label in case of doubt.
Product images: label if the AI changes colour, material, size, accessories or the usage situation. Colour correction, background, scaling, sharpening and compression are unproblematic.
AI testimonials: an AI person appearing as a real customer is a deepfake and must be labelled – plus a risk under competition law.
Audio and video: deepfakes must be labelled, e.g. voice clones in marketing videos or podcasts.
Chatbots: users must be able to recognise that they are interacting with an AI system.
Exceptions
Human review: texts are exempt if a person or organisation has reviewed them in substance and bears editorial responsibility. Cursory proofreading is not enough.
No deepfake criteria: fantasy, comic or clearly stylised motifs, icons, infographics and abstract graphics are typically not subject to labelling.
Technical adjustments (colour correction, background, scaling, sharpening, compression) are not subject to labelling.
Voluntary labelling can make sense, e.g. for advice with a legal or health reference, press releases or personal-looking texts such as columns.
How to label
The label must be clearly recognisable and visible at the latest at first contact – permanently for videos.
Image: firmly embedded, e.g. at the edge or in a corner.
Short video: visible throughout.
Longer video: at the beginning, repeatedly and after every cut.
Live stream: during the entire broadcast.
Audio: spoken notice at the beginning, additionally visual in players.
Text: placed consistently, e.g. above the text or at the headline.

Since June 2026 the EU Commission provides free icons "AI GENERATED", "AI MODIFIED" and a basic "AI" icon (use is voluntary). Own labels are permitted if firmly embedded in the file or shown as a clearly visible watermark.
Example texts
Text: "This text/article was created with the help of AI."
Audio: "This recording contains AI-generated content."
Image/video: EU icon "AI GENERATED" or "AI MODIFIED", or "AI-generated".
Who is responsible?
Technical marking (watermarks, metadata such as C2PA/IPTC) is the task of the AI provider. This extension reads such metadata on upload and labels automatically.
The visible label in the published content is the responsibility of the publishing organisation – i.e. yours.
Note on copyright

AI-generated texts and images are usually not protected by copyright. Protection can arise if a human edits the result substantially. A purely AI-generated logo can still be registered as a trademark.
